podcast.body: Blur bassist Alex James and drummer Dave Rowntree, both astronomy enthusiasts, approached the British Space Agency when they heard Britain was launching a Mars probe and proposed providing music to be broadcast upon a successful landing. The agency agreed, and on January 30, 2002, Blur recorded a specially commissioned instrumental called "Beagle II," based loosely on a mathematical sequence. The probe — named Beagle II — was launched on June 2, 2003, designed to land on the Martian surface in the equatorial region known as Isidis Planitia on Christmas Day 2003. After successfully separating from the parent spacecraft Mars Express in Martian orbit on December 19, Beagle II began its descent at 2:47 am London time on December 25 and was never heard from again, joining the long list of failed Martian probes. Blur's debut performance on Mars was never heard. "Essentially, we are going to play the first gig on Mars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Blur specifically wrote and recorded a song to be played by the Beagle II probe upon its successful landing on Mars. Had the mission been successful, this would have made Blur the first band to have music played on Mars. However, the probe was lost, and the song was never broadcast from the Martian surface. "When it phoned home, it was going to play a song, and that song was written specifically for Beagle II by Blur."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: This song was composed by Blur, instigated by Alex James, with the unique intention of being broadcast from Mars by the Beagle 2 space probe upon its planned landing on Christmas Day 2003. Although the probe was lost, the song remains a testament to the project. "It's Blur's Beagle 2 theme instigated by bass player Alex James."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
